reading.rtitle: Small Talk, Big Trust: Five Tips for Your First Meeting with a Foreign Partner
paras: Business is about people. Before a foreign brand signs an agreement with you, the people there want to trust you. Trust grows slowly, and it starts with small things. Here are five tips for your first meeting with a new partner.

Tip one: you should be punctual. Arrive five minutes early. In the United States, ten minutes late is not a small problem. Tip two: you should start with small talk. Ask about the trip, the hotel or the food in your city. You shouldn't talk about prices in the first minute.

Tip three: you shouldn't ask personal questions. Don't ask about money, age or religion. Work, travel, sport and food are safe topics. Tip four: you should bring business cards. At a networking event, people meet many new faces, and a card helps them remember your name.

Tip five is the most important: you should send a follow-up email the next day. Say thank you, write one thing from your conversation, and suggest the next step. A short follow-up shows that you listen and that you are reliable.
Should you be very formal all the time? No, you shouldn't. Be polite, smile and listen. A good business relationship starts with a good conversation.

listenings.text: Hi Gleice, it's Jennifer from NatureCare. Good news: Thomas Grant is coming to Sao Paulo next week for a pharmacy fair, and he would like to meet you on Tuesday at ten. A few tips, because I know Thomas well. First, you should be punctual. He hates waiting. Second, he loves football, so you should ask him about his team. That is great small talk for him. But you shouldn't talk about prices at lunch. He likes to talk about numbers in the office, not at the table. And you should bring some business cards, because he wants to introduce you to two distributors at the fair. Good luck, and call me after the meeting!

Hello, I'm Daniel Reed, and I teach networking to sales teams. Today, one topic: the follow-up email. Many people meet a great contact at an event, and then they do nothing. That is a mistake. You should send your follow-up in twenty-four hours, when the person still remembers your face. And it should be short: three or four sentences. First, say thank you. Then write one detail from your conversation, for example: I hope you enjoyed the feijoada. That shows you listened. Finally, suggest the next step: a call, a visit or a meeting. One more thing: you shouldn't attach ten files to the first email. One is enough. Trust grows with small, regular contact.
